topics.title: Linux Fundamentals
topics.summary: Core Linux command-line skills every DevOps engineer needs daily.
keyPoints: File system navigation, permissions (chmod/chown), and process management (ps, kill, top)
Shell scripting basics: variables, loops, conditionals in bash
Package management (apt/yum) and systemd for service management
Log inspection with grep, tail -f, journalctl

interviewQA.question: How would you find and kill a process that's consuming too much memory on a Linux server?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Use 'top' or 'htop' for a live view sorted by memory usage (Shift+M in top), or 'ps aux --sort=-%mem | head' to list the top memory consumers with their PIDs. Once you identify the offending PID, send it a graceful termination signal first with 'kill -15 <pid>' (SIGTERM), giving the process a chance to clean up, and only escalate to 'kill -9 <pid>' (SIGKILL) if it doesn't respond, since SIGKILL can leave resources like file locks in a bad state.
interviewQA.tip: Mention SIGTERM before SIGKILL — shows operational maturity, not just command memorization.

topics.title: Version Control with Git
topics.summary: Git workflows and branching strategies used in real DevOps pipelines.
keyPoints: Core commands: clone, branch, merge, rebase, cherry-pick
Branching strategies: Gitflow, trunk-based development, feature branches
Resolving merge conflicts and understanding the three-way merge
Git hooks for automating checks before commit/push

interviewQA.question: What's the difference between git merge and git rebase, and when would you use each?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: git merge combines two branches by creating a new merge commit that ties both histories together, preserving the exact history of how development happened, including parallel work. git rebase replays your branch's commits on top of another branch's latest state, producing a linear history without a merge commit, which is cleaner to read but rewrites commit hashes — meaning you should never rebase commits that have already been pushed and shared with others. A common pattern is rebasing local feature branches before merging into main to keep history clean, and merging (not rebasing) when integrating into shared/protected branches.
interviewQA.tip: The 'never rebase shared history' rule is the key safety point interviewers listen for.

topics.title: CI/CD Concepts
topics.summary: The principles behind continuous integration and continuous delivery/deployment pipelines.
keyPoints: CI: frequently merging and automatically building/testing code
CD (delivery): automated release-ready builds; CD (deployment): fully automated release to production
Pipeline stages: build, test, package, deploy, with gates between them
Common tools: Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Azure DevOps Pipelines

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Continuous Delivery means every change that passes the automated pipeline is proven to be deployable and packaged as a release-ready artifact, but a human still triggers the actual production release, often via a manual approval gate. Continuous Deployment goes one step further and removes that manual gate entirely — every change that passes all automated tests is automatically deployed to production with no human intervention. The choice depends on risk tolerance and how much confidence the team has in its automated test coverage.
interviewQA.tip: Give the one-line distinction clearly: delivery = ready to deploy, deployment = automatically deployed.

topics.title: Networking Basics for DevOps
topics.summary: Core networking concepts needed to design, debug, and secure infrastructure.
keyPoints: OSI/TCP-IP model, DNS resolution, and how load balancers route traffic
TCP vs UDP, and common ports (80, 443, 22, 3306, etc.)
Firewalls, security groups, and network ACLs
Basic troubleshooting: ping, traceroute, curl, netstat/ss

interviewQA.question: A web application is unreachable. Walk through your basic network troubleshooting steps.
interviewQA.modelAnswer: First confirm DNS resolves correctly (nslookup/dig) to the expected IP, then check basic reachability with ping, though ICMP is often blocked so that's not conclusive on its own. Next test the actual service port directly with curl or telnet/nc to the app's port (e.g., 443), which tells you whether it's a network/firewall issue versus an application issue. If the port is unreachable, check security groups/firewall rules and the load balancer's health check status; if the port is reachable but the app errors out, the problem has shifted from networking to the application layer.
interviewQA.tip: Structure the answer as a funnel: DNS -> reachability -> port -> app layer.

topics.title: Docker & Containerization
topics.summary: Packaging applications with their dependencies into portable, isolated containers.
keyPoints: Images (immutable layers) vs containers (running instances)
Dockerfile best practices: multi-stage builds, minimizing layers, .dockerignore
Container networking modes and volume mounting for persistent data
Image registries (Docker Hub, ECR, GCR) and image tagging strategies

interviewQA.question: Why would you use a multi-stage Dockerfile build, and what problem does it solve?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: A multi-stage build lets you use one stage with full build tools (compilers, SDKs, dev dependencies) to compile/build the application, and then copy only the final compiled artifacts into a much smaller final stage based on a minimal runtime image, discarding all the build-time bloat. This dramatically reduces the final image size (sometimes from over 1GB down to tens of MBs) and shrinks the attack surface by not shipping build tools or source code into production. It also avoids needing separate Dockerfiles for build vs runtime.
interviewQA.tip: Give a concrete example: Node/Java build stage -> slim Alpine runtime stage.

topics.title: Kubernetes Fundamentals
topics.summary: Orchestrating containerized workloads at scale with Kubernetes' core objects.
keyPoints: Pods, Deployments, Services, and how the control plane maintains desired state
ConfigMaps/Secrets for configuration, and readiness/liveness probes
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and resource requests/limits
Ingress controllers for routing external traffic into the cluster

interviewQA.question: What's the difference between a liveness probe and a readiness probe in Kubernetes?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: A liveness probe tells Kubernetes whether a container is still functioning; if it fails repeatedly, the kubelet kills and restarts the container, which is meant to recover from deadlocks or stuck states. A readiness probe tells Kubernetes whether the container is ready to receive traffic; if it fails, the pod is removed from the Service's load-balancing endpoints without restarting the container, which is meant for temporary states like still loading a large cache at startup. Misconfiguring liveness probes too aggressively is a common cause of crash-loop issues in production.
interviewQA.tip: Mention the crash-loop risk of a too-strict liveness probe — a real-world gotcha.

topics.title: Infrastructure as Code (Terraform)
topics.summary: Declaratively defining and managing cloud infrastructure as versioned code.
keyPoints: Providers, resources, and the declarative HCL syntax
State file: tracks real-world resource mapping; remote state (S3+DynamoDB, Terraform Cloud) for teams
Plan/apply workflow, and modules for reusable infrastructure components
Drift detection when real infrastructure diverges from the state file

interviewQA.question: Why is Terraform's state file important, and what problems can arise from managing it incorrectly?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Terraform's state file maps the resources declared in your configuration to actual real-world infrastructure IDs, which is how it knows what to create, update, or destroy on each apply. If two engineers apply changes using local state files simultaneously, they can corrupt each other's state or create duplicate/orphaned resources, which is why teams use remote state (e.g., S3 with DynamoDB for locking, or Terraform Cloud) to centralize and lock state during applies. If the state file is lost or gets out of sync with real infrastructure ('drift'), Terraform may try to recreate resources that already exist or fail to manage resources it no longer tracks.
interviewQA.tip: Mention remote state + locking (S3 + DynamoDB) as the standard team solution.

topics.title: Configuration Management (Ansible)
topics.summary: Automating server configuration and application deployment with agentless, idempotent playbooks.
keyPoints: Agentless architecture: connects over SSH, no daemon needed on managed nodes
Playbooks (YAML), tasks, and roles for reusable, organized automation
Idempotency: running a playbook repeatedly produces the same end state
Inventory files for grouping and targeting hosts

interviewQA.question: What does 'idempotency' mean in the context of Ansible, and why does it matter?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Idempotency means running the same Ansible playbook multiple times against the same system produces the same end result without unintended side effects — if a package is already installed or a file already has the right content, Ansible detects that and skips making a redundant change, reporting it as 'ok' rather than 'changed'. This matters because it makes automation safe to rerun after partial failures or on a schedule for drift correction, without worrying about duplicating actions or breaking things through repeated execution. Most built-in Ansible modules are idempotent by design; the risk is mainly in raw 'shell'/'command' tasks that execute arbitrary commands without that guarantee.
interviewQA.tip: Note that shell/command modules are the main idempotency risk — a good nuance to add.

topics.title: Multi-Cloud & Cloud Architecture (AWS/Azure/GCP)
topics.summary: Designing infrastructure that spans or migrates between major cloud providers.
keyPoints: Core service mapping across clouds: EC2/VM/Compute Engine, S3/Blob/Cloud Storage, IAM differences
Multi-cloud drivers: avoiding vendor lock-in, redundancy, regulatory/data-residency needs
Abstraction layers (Terraform, Kubernetes) to reduce cloud-specific coupling
Trade-offs: multi-cloud adds real operational complexity vs the resilience it buys

interviewQA.question: What are the real trade-offs of adopting a multi-cloud strategy versus committing to a single cloud provider?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Multi-cloud reduces vendor lock-in risk, can improve resilience against a provider-wide outage, and sometimes helps meet regulatory or data-residency requirements or negotiate better pricing. But it comes at a real cost: teams need expertise across multiple providers' services and IAM models, tooling and monitoring become more complex since each cloud has different APIs and quirks, and you often end up using only the lowest-common-denominator features to stay portable, missing out on provider-specific managed services. For most companies, a single primary cloud with a documented disaster-recovery plan is simpler and cheaper than true multi-cloud, which is best reserved for specific compliance or resilience requirements.
interviewQA.tip: A balanced, cost-aware answer beats blanket enthusiasm for multi-cloud — interviewers value pragmatism.

topics.title: Monitoring & Observability
topics.summary: Building visibility into distributed systems through metrics, logs, and traces.
keyPoints: The three pillars: metrics (Prometheus), logs (ELK/Loki), traces (Jaeger/OpenTelemetry)
SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets for defining and tracking reliability targets
Alerting on symptoms (user-facing impact) rather than just causes, to reduce noise
Dashboards (Grafana) for visualizing system health across services

interviewQA.question: What's the difference between monitoring and observability, and why does the distinction matter operationally?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Monitoring typically means watching predefined metrics and dashboards for known failure modes you anticipated in advance — it answers questions you already knew to ask. Observability is about instrumenting a system (rich structured logs, metrics, and distributed traces) so you can investigate and answer novel questions about problems you didn't anticipate, especially important in complex microservice architectures where failures emerge from unexpected interactions between services. In practice, observability is what lets an engineer trace a single slow request across a dozen microservices to find exactly which downstream call caused the latency, rather than just knowing 'overall latency is high'.
interviewQA.tip: Frame it as 'known unknowns' (monitoring) vs 'unknown unknowns' (observability).

topics.title: Site Reliability Engineering (SRE)
topics.summary: Applying software-engineering discipline to operations, balancing reliability and feature velocity.
keyPoints: Error budgets: the acceptable amount of unreliability, used to balance risk vs release velocity
Blameless postmortems for learning from incidents without punishing individuals
Toil reduction: automating repetitive operational work to free engineering time
On-call practices and incident response frameworks

interviewQA.question: How does an error budget change the conversation between a product team and an SRE team?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: An error budget quantifies acceptable unreliability (e.g., 99.9% uptime allows about 43 minutes of downtime per month) and turns reliability from a vague debate into a shared, numeric resource both teams can reason about. If the error budget is being spent responsibly and there's budget remaining, the product team can ship features and take reasonable risks; if the budget is exhausted, the SRE team has a data-backed mandate to pause risky releases and prioritize stability work instead, rather than relying on gut feeling or authority. This aligns incentives — reliability work isn't just 'ops slowing us down', it's a jointly agreed budget both sides manage together.
interviewQA.tip: Use the concrete 99.9% = ~43 min/month downtime math — precision impresses interviewers.

topics.title: Security & Compliance in DevOps (DevSecOps)
topics.summary: Embedding security practices directly into the CI/CD pipeline rather than bolting it on afterward.
keyPoints: Shift-left security: static analysis (SAST), dependency scanning, and secret scanning in CI
Least-privilege IAM policies and short-lived credentials over long-lived access keys
Secrets management (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) instead of hardcoded credentials
Compliance-as-code and automated policy enforcement (e.g., Open Policy Agent)

interviewQA.question: What does 'shift-left security' mean, and how would you implement it in a CI/CD pipeline?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Shift-left security means finding and fixing security issues as early as possible in the development lifecycle — ideally before code is even merged — rather than only scanning for vulnerabilities right before or after production deployment. In practice, this means adding automated static application security testing (SAST) and dependency vulnerability scanning as required steps in the CI pipeline that run on every pull request, plus secret-scanning to catch accidentally committed credentials before they ever reach a shared branch. The goal is to make the pipeline itself fail fast on security issues, the same way it fails on broken tests, so security becomes a routine part of every commit rather than a separate late-stage gate.
interviewQA.tip: Emphasize 'fails fast like a broken test' — ties security into normal engineering workflow.
